Photograph by REBECCA HALE, NGM staff Premium MAGAZINE INNOVATOR She studies ancient catastrophes to prevent future disasters This ‘disaster scientist’ is uncovering clues buried underwater that may save lives today. By Nina Strochlic Published April 23, 2020 • 2 min read This story appears in the May 2020 issue of National Geographic magazine. When Beverly Goodman was in elementary school, she gave a series of presentations on her favorite topic: disasters. She told her classmates about the eruption that buried Pompeii , the black plague , and famous shipwrecks like the Titanic and the Lusitania . Today, at 45, she’s a marine geoarchaeologist who excavates coastlines for clues to erosion, past tsunamis , and other disasters. “It’s funny now that I’m a disaster scientist, basically,” she says. “It all came together.” Human settlements have long been built around access to water. Goodman studies how coastal change affected our ancestors: Were people forced to leave? Did they find innovative ways to adapt to the changes? This knowledge, she says, can help us “prepare responsibly for what this landscape is going to look like in the future.” That was the case when Goodman and her team of scientists proved tsunamis had struck the coast of what is now Israel over the course of thousands of years. As options for the traditional chalet ski break have dwindled and prices risen, venturing to Europe’s far corners and beyond for a ski break can reap rewards. Costs are often lower, while luxury accommodation can be similarly priced to budget options in mainstream European ski resorts. As well as being potentially cheaper, skiing in territory off the beaten track can offer a rich cultural experience, plus better flight routes, less crowded slopes, sunnier days and a friendlier welcome. 1. Measles is a highly contagious disease that spreads through an infected person’s coughing, sneezing or breathing. Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and rash. pages.text: Bhutan is close to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies Skip to main content WHO/Bhutan Bhutan is close to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies © Credits Bhutan is close to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies 1 September 2026 Highlights Reading time: Rabies used to be a serious public health threat in Bhutan, especially in the southern border districts. Now, the country is on the verge of a major achievement: eliminating dog-mediated human rabies for good. This progress didn't happen overnight. It is the result of strong government leadership, years of sustained surveillance, rapid outbreak response, easy access to rabies vaccines after exposure, mass dog vaccination drives, better dog population management, and strong collaboration between human and animal health sectors. Bhutan has not recorded a single human rabies case since 2023—more than two years running. Having met WHO's requirements, Bhutan put together its official National Dossier on the Elimination of Dog-Mediated Human Rabies and asked WHO to independently validate this achievement in June 2026. From 18–21 August 2026, a team of international experts visited Bhutan to verify Bhutan's claim. They verified surveillance and programme data, carried out field visits, assessed programme implementation efforts, and met with key stakeholders across human and animal health sectors. The team confirmed Bhutan's progress and offered recommendations to help sustain Bhutan's achievements.

pages.text: Big Data Big Data Skip Navigation Big Data About Projects & Research Blog Posts Working Papers About About Projects & Research Blog Posts Working Papers About Big Data's mission is two-fold: 1) to apply cutting-edge data collection and analytics techniques to ensure the U.S. Census Bureau can maintain its high quality data products in a timely and efficient manner in the 21st Century; and 2) to create new products for public and business users. Our focus is on using data from both outside and inside the U.S. Census Bureau to improve current statistical products, provide new opportunities for research and innovation, and create new products and processes while reducing costs. What is Big Data? Big data is a term used to describe data sources that are fast-changing, large in both size and breadth of information, and come from sources other than surveys. Examples include retail and payroll transactions, satellite images, and "smart" devices. Big data also includes administrative data from federal, state, and local governments, as well as third party providers. Typically, big data is “found” or “observed”, in that it is collected passively as the digital exhausts of personal and commercial activities. Such seemingly disparate data sources and techniques can provide unique insights that were not easily observable previously. Combining big data from different sources for the U.S. Census Bureau’s research purposes and product development requires utilization of new techniques, including machine learning. This wilderness offers many recreation opportunities such as hiking, backpacking, rock climbing, photography and nature study. As a result, three districts have stopped Mass Drug Administration, advancing India’s LF elimination goal. 23 June 2026 Reading time: For generations, families across Bihar have lived under the burden of lymphatic filariasis (LF), a preventable neglected tropical disease that can cause lifelong disability, social stigma, and economic hardship. For the first time since launching Mass Drug Administration (MDA) in 2004, Bihar has successfully cleared its first Transmission Assessment Survey (TAS)—the standardized survey used to determine whether LF transmission has fallen below levels required to prevent new infection. Passing TAS allows the national programme to stop MDA and transition to post-MDA surveillance. The achievement is significant not only for Bihar but also for India’s goal of eliminating LF as a public health problem by 2027. As of May 2026, LF is endemic in 350 districts across 20 states and union territories in India. Bihar has faced one of the toughest challenges: all 38 districts and 592 implementation units are endemic for the disease. pages.text: Billions of T. rex likely roamed the Earth, paleontologists report | National Geographic Paleontologists figured out how many T. rex lived on Earth—and they found that about 20,000 would have been alive at any given time during a two- to three-million year timespan. Illustration by STOCKTREK IMAGES, Nat Geo Image Collection SCIENCE NEWS Billions of T. rex likely roamed the Earth, paleontologists report The iconic predator’s estimated abundance means the T. rex fossils we have today are exceedingly rare. By Michael Greshko Published April 19, 2021 • 6 min read If you traveled back in time 67 million years ago to ancient Montana, you’d be entering the realm of a tyrant: the iconic predator Tyrannosaurus rex . Before you venture into that lost world, though, you might want to know: On average, how close is the nearest T. rex to you? That might sound like an impossible thing to know—but after crunching through two decades’ worth of T. rex research, a new study provides estimates of the animal’s population density. In all likelihood, a T. rex would be within 15 miles of you, if not much closer. The new study, published last Thursday in Science , also translates these population densities into estimates for how many T. rex ever lived. On average, researchers estimate that some 20,000 T. rex lived at any one time and that about 127,000 generations of the dinosaurs lived and died. Those averages imply that a total of 2.5 billion T. rex lived in the species’ native North America, possibly as far north as Alaska and as far south as Mexico, over a two- to three-million-year timespan.

Bird Flu: Causes and How It Spreads Apr. 23, 2025 What to know Bird flu is caused by infection with avian influenza A viruses that usually spread between birds, not people. People rarely get bird flu, but when they do, it is most often after close, unprotected exposure (without wearing respiratory or eye protection) to birds or other animals infected with avian influenza A viruses. No person-to-person spread of bird flu has been identified in the United States at this time. Very rare, limited person to person spread has occurred in other countries. Causes Bird flu is a disease caused by avian influenza A viruses that usually spread between birds. Avian influenza A viruses have caused sporadic human infections in multiple countries, including the United States. Most human infections have happened after exposure to infected animals. Avian influenza A viruses that have infected humans Five subtypes of avian influenza A viruses are known to have infected people. These are called A/H5, A/H6, A/H7, A/H9, and A/H10 viruses. Among these, A/H5, A/H7 and A/H9 viruses have caused the most human infections. Keep Reading Avian Influenza

pages.text: Birds, Bats and Bugs: The Teeming World Above Our Heads Skip to main content There's More to That A Smithsonian magazine special report Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Photos by malik / Jim via Adobe Stock / Dina Litovsky and public domain The skies above us are filled with legions of migrating birds, bats, bugs and microbes. And yet we know little about their movements and intentions, mostly because this ethereal world has largely been inaccessible for research. But new technologies are providing a window into how animals use their aerial habitat to travel and hunt. The burgeoning field is called “aeroecology,” and researchers are revealing just how substantially humans are altering the world overhead—with deadly consequences for flying animals. The new insights are giving us ways to make the air safer for these creatures. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with Dustin Partridge of the New York City Bird Alliance as he directs the intermittent shutdown of the iconic Tribute in Light to protect disoriented birds during 9/11 this year. Every week, a group of elderly birders spend hours hunkering down inside a wooden hide in the English countryside, peering through binoculars as they excitedly share what they spot. An oystercatcher's long, bright beak probing the pebbled ground; two great crested grebes bobbing in the water, their plumed heads poised. Most of these birdwatchers have difficulty recalling what happened earlier that day, and might struggle to follow a conversation. But they become animated when swapping notes on the birds that fill the sky around Forge Mill Lake in the UK's West Midlands. Among them is 78-year-old Harold*. He loved the outdoors when he was younger, but more recently dementia has made him withdrawn and anxious. His daughter Lucy* brought him here, hoping that the change of scenery and peaceful lake might be good for him. After an apprehensive start, Harold began smiling when someone pointed out a robin and enjoyed watching the ducks splashing in the water. Why is major improvement work taking place at Birmingham New Street? Network Rail is carrying out major engineering work at Birmingham New Street this Christmas as part of a 3-year, £13m programme to renew ageing overhead line equipment through the station. The overhead line equipment powers electric trains through the station. Much of this equipment dates back to the 1960s and now needs to be replaced to help reduce faults and improve the long-term reliability of journeys through Birmingham New Street. When is the work taking place? The first phase of work will take place from Christmas Eve (Thursday 24 December) to Bank Holiday Monday (28 December) 2026 . The principal attraction for rock collectors here is fire agate. Fire agate is a relatively new gemstone, only identified and formally recognized in the 1930s. It has the color play of precious opal with gem quality reds, greens, and blues. The desert regions of Arizona, southern California, and central Mexico are the only areas of the world where fire agate is known to occur. Through collaborative efforts, state and local entities that provide employment support services can maximize employment and economic advancement outcomes for disabled people. Blending, braiding, and sequencing (BBS) are innovative strategies that maximize the efficient and effective use of federal funds across systems to help people with disabilities secure and maintain CIE. Defining BBS Blending occurs when dollars from multiple funding streams combine to create a single “pot” of commingled dollars that can fund an initiative or purchase more specific services. Blending involves pooling funds from multiple sources to support a common goal, such that each individual funding source gives up its program identity. Typically, states or regions need explicit authorization by statute or regulation to allow the blending of funds. pages.description: As a Syrian glassmaker created his wares in Damascus, watching his craft reminded this reporter to slow down and enjoy the moment.
pages.text: Blissful moment as Syria glass blower braves scorching temps : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Blissful moment as Syria glass blower braves scorching temps As a Syrian glassmaker created his wares in Damascus, watching his craft reminded this reporter to slow down and enjoy the moment. Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps September 30, 2026 1:51 PM ET Emily Feng Emily Feng/NPR Our world as journalists can move fast; every day there's breaking news from all corners of the world, and we scramble to stay on top of multiple threads of information each day. That is why I loved watching this glassmaker just outside the historic Old City in Damascus. In 100 degree summer heat, he patiently shaped cup after glass cup in the blistering furnace in front of him, seemingly impervious to the temperature. Time seemed to matter less than the process of melting and stretching the hot, melted glass. He made cups and oil jars and decorative lamps in a variety of jewel colors, using techniques and styles that have not changed for decades. Watching his craft reminded me to slow down and enjoy the moment, too. Sponsor Message Even though his shop was right on the edge of the Old City of Damascus, it was largely empty. Syria's nearly 14-year civil war has ended, but the economy is still struggling, while inflation has ratcheted up the cost of living in the last year. Even a glass can be a luxury for some.
